name: Bach-Weyl Ring
description: The static vacuum field of a thin circular ring of matter in Weyl's class, written down by Rudolf Bach in 1922 in a paper with a supplement by Hermann Weyl. Its Weyl potential is Newton's potential of a hoop, a complete elliptic integral. The ring is a naked singularity that lies a finite distance away from outside and an infinite distance away from inside.
convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ and the ring's radius $a$ are lengths. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Rudolf Bach was a nom de plume [goenner2004]. The man behind it was Rudolf Förster, a mathematician whose thesis of 1908 treated Riemann's P-function, and who worked for Krupp [goenner2004]. Krupp, in Hubert Goenner's words, "did not like his employees using their free time on something as academical as research in gravitation and unified field theory" [goenner2004]. Under his own name Förster wrote to Albert Einstein on 11 November 1917 to propose a metric with an antisymmetric part that would hold the electromagnetic field [goenner2004]. As Bach he published a paper in 1922, with a supplement by Hermann Weyl, on static fields with an axis of symmetry written out explicitly [bach1922]. Gernot Neugebauer and David Petroff put it into English in 2012 [bach2012, semerak2016].¶Weyl had supplied the recipe in 1917, when he reduced the vacuum field equations of such a field to two functions, $\psi$ and $\gamma$, of his coordinates $\rho$ and $z$ [weyl1917, antoci2001]. The first solves Laplace's equation in a flat space of three dimensions, so any Newtonian potential with an axis of symmetry will do, and the second follows from the first by an integral [antoci2001]. Bach fed the recipe the potential of two rods laid along the axis and got two bodies at rest, with a singular stretch of axis between them that Weyl took for the stress holding them apart [antoci2001]. His other potential was that of a hoop, a thin circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $a$ [bach1922, semerak2016]. Newton's potential of a hoop is a complete elliptic integral, $\psi = -2m\,\mathrm{K}(\kappa)/(\pi l_2)$, with $m = GM/c^2$, $l_2$ the greatest distance from the point to the ring, and $\kappa$ running from zero on the axis to one at the ring [semerak2016].¶How does space look close to the hoop? C. Hoenselaers found in 1995 that the space around the ring is strongly anisotropic, unlike the space around a straight wire [hoenselaers1995, semerak2016]. The full list of its measures waited until 2016, when Oldřich Semerák worked through them [semerak2016]. From outside, in the plane of the ring, the proper distance to it is finite, and from inside, across the disc within it, the distance is infinite [semerak2016]. The circumference of the ring is infinite, and so is the area of the disc [semerak2016]. A small circle looped around the ring has an outer half whose length shrinks to zero and an inner half whose length diverges, and Semerák calls the lot "weird" [semerak2016].¶What does a falling stone do there? Three physicists at Campinas, L. A. D'Afonseca, P. S. Letelier, and S. R. Oliveira, let test particles fall around the ring in 2005 and found that the ones approaching it are led to its inner rim "but never hit the ring" [dafonseca2005]. The inner side attracts them and lies too far away to reach, so the fall takes an infinite proper time [dafonseca2005, semerak2016]. Light sent from the centre toward the ring takes an infinite time $t$ as well [semerak2016]. The three suspected a strong hoop tension along the ring, since something has to keep a static ring from falling in on itself, and in general relativity tension gravitates as density does [dafonseca2005].¶At $a = 0$ the ring is the Curzon-Chazy particle, whose singularity Susan Scott and Peter Szekeres showed in 1986 to have the structure of a ring itself [semerak2016, scott1986a]. Set around Schwarzschild's hole, the ring has served Semerák, T. Zellerin, and M. Žáček since 1999 as a model of a black hole with heavy matter circling it [semerak1999, semerak2016]. A heavy or a close ring, M. Basovník and Semerák found in 2016, makes the Kretschmann scalar negative in regions inside the horizon [basovnik2016]. Semerák advises anyone doing such work to keep clear of the ring itself or to give it some thickness, and suspects that "a more adequate coordinate representation and interpretation of this source" is still to be found [semerak2016].

related.text: The ring with its radius shrunk to nothing. At $a = 0$ Newton's potential of the hoop is that of a point, and the metric is Curzon and Chazy's [semerak2016].
Static discs in Weyl's class, built on Newton's potential of a disc as the ring is on that of a hoop.

A Weyl field too, built on Newton's potential of a rod on the axis [antoci2001]. M. Basovník and Oldřich Semerák set the ring around Schwarzschild's hole and found the curvature inside the horizon strongly changed [basovnik2016].
Kerr's singularity is a ring as well, and a spinning one. Oldřich Semerák compared the two and found Kerr's ring the simpler [semerak2016].

Extremal black holes strung evenly around a circle, in the limit of infinitely many, make a ring with the same Newtonian potential. Its distance from the centre is finite where Bach and Weyl's is infinite [semerak2016].
A Weyl field too, built on the potential of Schwarzschild's rod with a quadrupole term added, where Bach and Weyl's is built on a hoop's.
The Weyl field of a rod on the axis. Bach's other field of 1922 is built from two such rods [antoci2001].

coordinates.name: Weyl

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the ring, measured at spatial infinity
Radius of the ring in Weyl's coordinates, a length; the ring is the circle $\rho = a$, $z = 0$, and $a = 0$ is the Curzon-Chazy particle
Greatest distance from the point to the ring in the flat space of Weyl's coordinates; the least distance is $l_1 = \sqrt{(\rho - a)^2 + z^2}$
Parameter of the two elliptic integrals, the square of their modulus; $1 - \kappa = l_1^2/l_2^2$, so $\kappa = 0$ on the axis and $\kappa \to 1$ at the ring

Weyl's first function, with $c^2\psi$ Newton's potential of a uniform ring of mass $M$ and radius $a$; $\mathrm{K}(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}d\alpha/\sqrt{1 - \kappa\sin^2\alpha}$ is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. It solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_\rho^2\psi + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\partial_\rho\psi + \partial_z^2\psi = 0$, in the flat space of $\rho$, $\phi$, and $z$; on the axis $\psi = -m/\sqrt{z^2 + a^2}$, and at the ring $\psi \to -\infty$ as $(m/\pi a)\ln(l_1/8a)$

Weyl's second function, with $\mathrm{E}(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1 - \kappa\sin^2\alpha}\,d\alpha$ the complete elliptic integral of the second kind; it is fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho\psi\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z\psi\right)^2\right)$ and $\partial_z\gamma = 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_z\psi$, and is zero on the axis, which is then free of conical singularities

coordinates.convention: We use Weyl's canonical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, and write $\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{E}$ for the complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kinds with parameter $\kappa$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Toroidal

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the ring, measured at spatial infinity
Radius of the ring in Weyl's coordinates, a length; the ring is the limit $\zeta \to \infty$, and a surface of constant $\zeta$ is a torus around it
Parameter of the two elliptic integrals, the square of their modulus; $\kappa = 0$ on the axis and $\kappa \to 1$ at the ring

Weyl's first function, with $c^2\psi$ Newton's potential of a uniform ring of mass $M$ and radius $a$; $\mathrm{K}(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}d\alpha/\sqrt{1 - \kappa\sin^2\alpha}$ is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. It solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_\zeta\left(\dfrac{\sinh\zeta}{\cosh\zeta - \cos\sigma}\partial_\zeta\psi\right) + \partial_\sigma\left(\dfrac{\sinh\zeta}{\cosh\zeta - \cos\sigma}\partial_\sigma\psi\right) = 0$, and at the ring $\psi \to -\infty$ as $-(m/\pi a)\,\zeta$

Weyl's second function, with $\mathrm{E}(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1 - \kappa\sin^2\alpha}\,d\alpha$ the complete elliptic integral of the second kind; it is fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_\zeta\gamma = \dfrac{\sinh\zeta}{\cosh\zeta - \cos\sigma}\left(\left(1 - \cosh\zeta\cos\sigma\right)\left(\left(\partial_\zeta\psi\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\sigma\psi\right)^2\right) - 2\sinh\zeta\sin\sigma\,\partial_\zeta\psi\,\partial_\sigma\psi\right)$ and $\partial_\sigma\gamma = \dfrac{\sinh\zeta}{\cosh\zeta - \cos\sigma}\left(\sinh\zeta\sin\sigma\left(\left(\partial_\zeta\psi\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\sigma\psi\right)^2\right) + 2\left(1 - \cosh\zeta\cos\sigma\right)\partial_\zeta\psi\,\partial_\sigma\psi\right)$, and is zero on the axis, which is then free of conical singularities

coordinates.convention: We use toroidal coordinates $(t, \zeta, \sigma, \phi)$ about the ring, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\zeta$ and $\sigma$ pure numbers, and write $\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{E}$ for the complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kinds with parameter $\kappa$. Weyl's canonical coordinates are $\rho = a\sinh\zeta/(\cosh\zeta - \cos\sigma)$ and $z = a\sin\sigma/(\cosh\zeta - \cos\sigma)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Oblate Spheroidal

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the ring, measured at spatial infinity
Radius of the ring in Weyl's coordinates, a length; the ring is the circle $\xi = 0$, $\eta = 0$, the rim of the disc $\xi = 0$ it spans

Parameter of the two elliptic integrals in Landen's form, the square of $(l_2 - l_1)/(l_2 + l_1)$ with $l_1$ and $l_2$ the least and greatest distances from the point to the ring in the flat space of Weyl's coordinates; $\kappa = 0$ on the axis and $\kappa = 1$ on the disc $\xi = 0$ at its rim, the ring

Weyl's first function, with $c^2\psi$ Newton's potential of a uniform ring of mass $M$ and radius $a$; $\mathrm{K}(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}d\alpha/\sqrt{1 - \kappa\sin^2\alpha}$ is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. It solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_\xi\left(\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\partial_\xi\psi\right) + \partial_\eta\left(\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\partial_\eta\psi\right) = 0$, and on the axis $\psi = -m/\left(a\sqrt{1 + \xi^2}\right)$; in Weyl's chart the same function is written with the parameter $1 - l_1^2/l_2^2$

Weyl's second function, with $\mathrm{E}(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1 - \kappa\sin^2\alpha}\,d\alpha$ the complete elliptic integral of the second kind; it is fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_\xi\gamma = \dfrac{1 - \eta^2}{\xi^2 + \eta^2}\left(\xi\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\left(\partial_\xi\psi\right)^2 - \xi\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\left(\partial_\eta\psi\right)^2 - 2\eta\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\partial_\xi\psi\,\partial_\eta\psi\right)$ and $\partial_\eta\gamma = \dfrac{1 + \xi^2}{\xi^2 + \eta^2}\left(\eta\left(1 + \xi^2\right)\left(\partial_\xi\psi\right)^2 - \eta\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\left(\partial_\eta\psi\right)^2 + 2\xi\left(1 - \eta^2\right)\partial_\xi\psi\,\partial_\eta\psi\right)$, and is zero on the axis, which is then free of conical singularities

coordinates.convention: We use oblate spheroidal coordinates $(t, \xi, \eta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\xi$ and $\eta$ pure numbers, and write $\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{E}$ for the complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kinds with parameter $\kappa$. Weyl's canonical coordinates are $\rho = a\sqrt{(1 + \xi^2)(1 - \eta^2)}$ and $z = a\xi\eta$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
